Field studies of Dwarf musk deer (Moschus berezovskii) have provided detailed documentation of early life stages under natural conditions. Newborn fawns, which are highly precocial, emerge with a wet weight at birth of 524 grams [Wwb = 524 grams], a measurement reflecting the substantial maternal investment characteristic of solitary forest ungulates. This initial mass supports the fawn through the critical neonatal period, during which it remains hidden in dense undergrowth while the mother forages nearby. The weaning process, marking the end of nutritional dependence on milk, is completed at approximately 75 days after birth [tx = approximately 75 days after birth] under the typical body temperature regime of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], a timing that aligns with the seasonal flush of tender herbaceous vegetation in their montane habitat. The relatively short nursing period is notable given the species’ solitary and cryptic lifestyle.

As juveniles transition toward independence, their growth trajectory is shaped by the energetic demands of a harsh, seasonal environment. The time since birth at puberty, a milestone defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs at 540 days after birth [tp = 540 days after birth] when maintained at a core body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This two-stage maturation schedule—nearly one and a half years from birth—is remarkably prolonged compared to similarly sized ruminants and likely reflects the slow pace of life associated with low-resource, temperate forests. Following puberty, individuals continue to add mass and refine their foraging skills before venturing into the breeding population. The delayed reproductive onset is thought to reduce intraspecific competition for territory and mates among these solitary, forest-dwelling animals.

The reproductive biology of female dwarf musk deer is tightly constrained by their small body size and seasonal metabolic demands. Within the thermal environment of a typical resting state, measured at 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], gestation extends over a period of 197 days [tg = 197 days]. This relatively long gestation, compared to other caprines of similar mass, is consistent with the production of a single, well-developed offspring that is capable of independent locomotion within hours of birth. The prolonged intrauterine development appears to be an adaptation to the cool montane forests they inhabit, allowing the foetus to achieve a high degree of physiological maturity before facing the challenges of the external environment. Successful parturition is thus timed to coincide with the onset of the spring growing season.

Adult body size in this sexually dimorphic species is a key determinant of reproductive output and survival. The ultimate wet weight of females reaches approximately 12,800 grams [Wwi = approximately 12,800 grams], a modest mass that positions them among the smallest of the musk deer. This ceiling on body size is closely linked to their specialized browsing diet and the need for agility in steep, rocky terrain. From a life-history perspective, a female producing a single fawn per year from a litter size of one [Ri = single fawn per year from a litter size of one], with a reproductive frequency of one event per year [F_R_i = one event per year], operates at a very low annual fecundity. This strategy, while limiting population growth, is well-suited to a stable, low-predation environment where juvenile survival is relatively high.

Maximum lifespan remains one of the more uncertain demographic parameters for Dwarf musk deer in the wild, though available data provide useful estimates. The maximum recorded longevity is approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years], a figure that carries some uncertainty given the challenges of tracking solitary, secretive individuals over extended periods in rugged habitats at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. When measured under the standard metabolic conditions characteristic of active adults (38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]), this lifespan is comparatively long for a mammal of its size, aligning more closely with larger-bodied deer species. The extended post-reproductive period in some individuals may contribute to social stability and territory maintenance, though direct evidence remains sparse. Continued monitoring of marked populations will be necessary to refine these longevity estimates.
